model_note.S:
CC: My left calf cramps whenever I walk a couple of blocks.

HPI: 59-year-old male. Three months of exertional left calf pain. Pain is localized to the left calf. No radiation. Cramping tightness. 6/10 and limits walking. Resolves within 3 minutes of rest. Walking threshold decreased from six to two blocks. Provoked earlier by brisk walking or hills. Standing rest suffices without lumbar flexion. Not provoked by standing alone. Stretching ineffective. No earlier episodes.

PMH: Hypertension and hyperlipidemia. No known diabetes.

PSH: Appendectomy at 19.

Meds: Lisinopril 20 mg daily; stopped atorvastatin 20 mg 6 months ago because of cost.

SH: Current tobacco: 35 pack-years. Approximately one beer weekly. No recreational drugs. Warehouse supervisor; walking duties limited. Lives with husband; transport available.

FH: Father: myocardial infarction at 54. Mother: type 2 diabetes. Younger sister: hypertension.

Allergies: Penicillin: hives, no respiratory reaction.

ROS: Cardiovascular: No chest pain. No dyspnea. No edema. Musculoskeletal: Occasional nonradiating low-back ache after work. No hip or knee pain. Exertional left calf cramping. Neurologic: No numbness. No paresthesias. No focal weakness. No rest pain or nonhealing wounds.
model_note.O:
Vitals: BP 148/86 mmHg, P 78 bpm, R 16 rpm, T 98.4 F oral, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 10", Wt 194 lbs

General: Alert, comfortable at rest, without respiratory distress.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm without murmur. Left dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses 1+; right pedal pulses 2+.
Lungs: Breath sounds clear bilaterally.
Extremities: Left foot slightly cooler than right; capillary refill 3 seconds left and 2 seconds right. No edema or calf asymmetry.
Skin: Reduced hair over the left lower leg; no ulcer or tissue loss on inspected legs and feet.
Musculoskeletal: No focal calf or knee tenderness. Mild bilateral lumbar paraspinal tenderness. Ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion 5/5 bilaterally.
Neurologic: Light touch intact in both feet.
Osteopathic: L3 bilateral lumbar paraspinal tissue texture change and tenderness.
A: 1. Peripheral artery disease with intermittent claudication
2. Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
P: 1. Obtain resting ankle-brachial indices and assess cardiovascular risk; use exercise ABI if resting results are nondiagnostic. If PAD is confirmed, discuss single antiplatelet and high-intensity statin therapy after contraindication review, structured walking, smoking cessation and daily foot care. Address refill cost; review in 2 weeks. Sudden persistent pain, pallor, coldness or weakness needs emergency care.

2. If vascular testing does not explain symptoms, reassess posture dependence and neurologic findings; pursue lumbar evaluation as indicated. Encourage tolerable activity and explain emergency bladder, saddle-sensation or weakness symptoms.

3. If a muscular cause remains likely after vascular assessment, use relative rest, gentle rehabilitation and safe analgesia rather than forcing painful exercise. Explain a gradual return to work and activity after vascular causes have been assessed.
